extracted.intended_audience: authors of mathematical research papers (particularly applied mathematics/engineering researchers and graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for planning, structuring, writing, and typesetting academic papers with substantial mathematical content, aimed at making the paper readable, self-contained, and publication-ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a particular audience in mind; e.g., your fellow students, the experts, conference attendees, undergraduates, or your grandparents, and speak to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The choice of audience determines prior knowledge you can assume and the level of detail to provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the main point(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the main point (or a small number of main points) of the paper? Why should this paper exist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the core contribution before writing; this drives organization and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a table of contents / outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a table of contents. For each section and subsection, write down a few bullet points about their intended contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning sections/subsections as bullet points helps keep each unit focused and aligned with the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect your results before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down precise statements of the main theorems and lemmas. Be sure that you have proofs or are fully confident you can produce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting formal results early avoids drafting around incomplete or uncertain claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation management
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the notation that you will be using on a separate sheet. Check for consistency, conflicts, and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick convenient notation and apply it consistently; when multiple authors are involved, early agreement on notation reduces errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick your preferred terminology and follow it (e.g., links/arcs/edges; agents/sensors/nodes; multiagent/multi-agent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent in grammatical/spelling choices to minimize reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical document structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A common structure: Abstract; Introduction; The Model; Preliminaries (optional); Results (usually 1–4 sections); Conclusions; Appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary preliminaries that delay reaching the core; use a clear, conventional structure unless there's a reason not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section size and theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections should be of manageable size, with one clear theme in each section. Ideal unit lengths are 1–3 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break long sections into subsections/subsubsections; headings act as signposts and should be chosen carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start/end section guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every section (or subsection) should start with guidance on what is to happen next and end with a summary of what has been accomplished (and possibly what is coming next).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrases like 'We will now...' at the start and short summaries at the end to keep readers oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modules and subheadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize subsections into 'modules' such as introduction, theorems, lemmas, proofs, definitions, assumptions, explanations, figures, tables, examples, and counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delineate modules with subheadings or paragraph structure so readers can scan and follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: be crisp and focused
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be crisp and to the point. Do not give the history, background motivation, or engage in marketing. Use simple, declarative sentences and minimal mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A usual structure is 'We consider ...' followed by 'We show that ...'. A permissible variation is to begin with application motivation or relation to seminal work, but keep it concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: frame the paper early
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by framing the paper (e.g., 'In this paper we address the problem of ...') rather than beginning with background/history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After framing, give motivation and a contextual comparison with related work (don't just list papers). Provide a succinct preview of the main results and contributions; end with an organization paragraph ('The rest of the paper is organized as follows...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions: add value beyond summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a conclusions section that merely repeats the introduction. Instead, emphasize key ideas from the body that were hard to explain earlier and discuss conjectures, open problems, and plausible extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conclusions to suggest directions beyond the paper rather than duplicate content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appendices appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appendices for complicated proofs that break continuity, or for simple but lengthy proofs necessary for completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main text should be self-contained: state lemmas used in the main text even if proofs are in the appendix, and avoid using notation defined only in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless you have tremendous confidence in your writing skills, break long sentences into multiple short sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter sentences reduce parsing difficulty, especially when mathematics are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent voice and pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a voice and pronoun and use it consistently. Active voice ('We will show...') is preferable to passive; 'we' is preferable to 'I'; avoid 'one'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive voice may be used sparingly to skip elementary arguments (e.g., 'It can be shown that...') but provide a hint or reference for non-elementary omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallel constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parallel grammatical constructions to improve clarity (e.g., present paired statements using the same syntactic structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallelism aids readability and reduces ambiguity in comparisons or dichotomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't prove on the computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not try to write up a proof directly on the computer; write mathematical pieces with pencil and paper first, check correctness, then typeset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, mark substantive revisions on printouts rather than editing directly on-screen for nontrivial changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce linear structure in arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for linear (forward) proofs and arguments; avoid presenting proofs that mix backward and forward reasoning because they are hard to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proofs were discovered backwards, reorder them to a forward structure for exposition; if appendix material is used, ensure the proof is thought of as linear when the appendix is conceptually inserted at the right spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols near their first use
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you have defined every symbol you use, preferably right before or right after its first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some general symbols may be defined early, but most definitions should appear close to first use to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theorem/lemma statements short and crisp
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem or lemma statements should be as short and crisp as possible; define relevant terms and symbols before the formal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put discussions of consequences inside formal statements; present consequences outside the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mnemonic labels for conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce mnemonic terms or labels (e.g., 'the degeneracy condition (3.1)') rather than referring to 'Condition (3.1)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mnemonic labels make subsequent references easier for the reader to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize proof ideas outside proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the main idea or flow of a proof outside the formal proof environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether a paragraph is motivation, explanation, handwaving, or rigorous to avoid confusing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have theorem precede the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a 'magician' trick of assembling facts and then declaring 'We have thus proved the theorem.' The theorem statement should precede its proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be upfront: present the statement first, then the proof, with an outline if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete examples and counterexamples to motivate assumptions and show why certain conditions are necessary (or overly restrictive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples clarify why assumptions exist and when results fail or can be relaxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures with informative captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures to illustrate results and provide intuition. Captions may be substantial and self-contained, possibly demonstrating a graphical example or proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures should aid understanding; a long explanatory caption is acceptable if it helps the reader interpret the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize reader effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Always aim to minimize the reader's effort (avoid sudden references to terms defined many pages earlier; include reminders where necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert reminders like 'Recall the definition cn = n / log n [cf. Eq. (3.2)].' to reduce re-scanning and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise about quantifier scope to avoid ambiguity (e.g., 'for every n, we have n < c, for some c' can be read as ∀n ∃c vs ∃c ∀n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out intended quantifier order or rephrase to eliminate ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify big-O and order notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Order-of-magnitude notation (e.g., 'T = O(nd)') can be ambiguous: distinguish between constants that may or may not depend on parameters like d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the intended interpretation explicitly when the default may be unclear (e.g., whether the constant c can depend on d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit sentences to remove unnecessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Read every sentence to identify and remove unnecessary words or clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But retain words like 'then' or 'that' when they improve parsing; be judicious rather than dogmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'then' and 'that' for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Include 'then' or 'that' where needed to make sentences grammatically clear (e.g., 'If n is odd, then n is nonzero'; 'Assume that n is odd').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'that' when redundant or clumsy, e.g., 'Assume n is a number that divides m' is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make pointer words unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure pronouns and pointers like 'it', 'this', 'that', 'which' clearly reference the intended antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous pointers lead to reader confusion—rewrite for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize references to specific items
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words such as 'Section', 'Chapter', 'Theorem' when referring to a specific numbered item (e.g., 'Theorem 1 in Section 2').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a consistent capitalization convention; use 'Eq. (3.1)' and similar short forms for equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation conventions (e.g., 'e.g.', 'cf.')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas with 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' in American English (e.g., 'An integer, e.g., the number 3.'), while 'cf.' is often used without a following comma ('A surprising result, cf. [6],').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent with punctuation conventions; pay attention to commas in introductory clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation punctuation convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the convention of placing commas and periods inside quotes (e.g., 'this is a success,' not 'this is a success'.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not logically necessary, this is generally more pleasing in American typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'that' vs 'which'
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and apply the conventional rules for using 'that' and 'which'; sometimes only one is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use restrictive vs nonrestrictive clause rules to decide which word fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid labeling things 'easy/trivial/obvious'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the phrases 'easy', 'trivial', 'obvious', etc., which can be dismissive and unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a step is omitted, indicate why or provide a reference/hint so readers are not left guessing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat math in sentences as ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sentences that include math readable as ordinary sentences (e.g., avoid 'for every k = 1, 2, ..., n' as it reads awkwardly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'for every k ∈ {1,2,...,n}' or 'for k = 1,2,...,n' to maintain grammatical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with math symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a short lead-in phrase or name the object in words before using the symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using ∃ and ∀ in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the symbols ∃ or ∀ in the text; write 'there exists' or 'for all' instead (∈ is acceptable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual quantifiers read more smoothly and avoid terse symbolic clutter in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary symbols and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce unnecessary symbols (e.g., say 'every prime number is odd' rather than 'every prime number p is odd' if p is not needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce shorthand only for expressions that appear multiple times; avoid shorthand for things used only once or twice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed equations as sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuate sentences involving displayed mathematics as you would ordinary sentences (include commas/periods where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves flow and readability and reinforces the sentence structure around displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't assert uniqueness without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not say 'the optimal solution' if uniqueness has not been proved; instead say 'an optimal solution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about existence vs uniqueness to avoid misleading readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting: emphasize readability of theorem environments
rubrics_metrics.description: LaTeX's default italic theorem environments may be less effective; consider alternatives (e.g., boxed theorems) to focus reader attention without compromising readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a style that highlights results and improves scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting: highlight newly introduced terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight newly introduced terms using italics or boldface so they are easy to spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boldface is visually easier to spot, but italics is the common convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inline fractions when they shrink font
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inline fractions like (x+2)/(x+3) rendered inline as x+2/x+3; prefer (x + 2)/(x + 3) to maintain legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use displayed fractions or slash form to avoid cramped inline typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break and align multiline equations correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and apply the rules for breaking and aligning multiline equations; good alignment greatly aids parsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established LaTeX environments and spacing rules for multi-line displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insert spaces in math for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert spaces to help the reader (e.g., write f(x) < y, ∀ y > 0 rather than f(x) < y, ∀y > 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Use explicit spacing commands (e.g., '
obreakspace' or '\,') where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct spacing after abbreviations in LaTeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of spacing issues after periods (e.g., 'Eq.' may produce extra space); use backslash-space '\ ' after period to get better spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small spacing fixes improve the aesthetic flow of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper spacing in set and conditional notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer '{x | x ∈ R}' with spacing (use '\mid' or '\,|\,') and 'E[X | Y]' rather than 'E[X|Y]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spaces around '|' make complex expressions easier to parse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer scalable parentheses and norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\big' or other scalable delimiters for outer parentheses (e.g., \big( x + y(t + 2) \big) ) and prefer '\|x\|' (\| \|) over '||x||'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better delimiters avoid ambiguous nesting and improve visual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set 'inf', 'sup', 'max' in roman font
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset operators like 'inf', 'sup', and 'max' in roman font, not math-italic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows typographical conventions and distinguishes operators from variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a stylized R for real numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \mathbb{R} or another fancy form for the real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow common notation to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add small horizontal spaces in integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Add small horizontal spaces inside formulas (e.g., use '\,' in integrals to change \int x dx to \int x\,dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small spacing adjustments improve readability in dense formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define LaTeX macros for complicated notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If using complicated notation (e.g., ˆa(k)_{ij}(t)), define a macro so you can change notation globally later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macros simplify later stylistic changes and maintain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct left-quote entry in LaTeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember left quotes require two keystrokes in LaTeX (``) to produce proper opening quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper quotes improve typography and readability.
